segments.text: Welcome to the last line of defense. I'm Seth Jones, your host and president of the Defense and Security Department at the Center for Strategic and International Studies. And I'm joined today by Ambassador Edgard Kagan, the

Freeman Chair in China Studies at the Center for Strategic International Studies. And quite relevant for our discussion today. He served as the US ambassador to Malaysia for presidents Trump and Biden and also as special assistant to the president and senior

director for East Asia and Oceanana at the National Security Council. Thank you so much for joining us today. >> Thank you so much for having me, Seth. It's a great pleasure to be on the last line of defense. >> All right. Well, um I wanted to start

have this actually conversation after the meeting between President Trump and Xiinping partly to let a few days go by and to talk about sort of what's come out of it. So let me just start off with sort of a bottom line upfront question

for you which is what are your takeaways main takeaways now from the Trump she meeting and what did they respectively get out of it from your perspective? >> So I think that your basic gist that basic idea of let's wait till the dust

settles and look to decide sort of what really happened I think is just right. Um I mean it's very clear that there was a lot of fever speculation both before the visit and during the visit itself and then immediately as the president

was taking off about sort of what happened what the big takeaways were uh what was agreed or not agreed upon. I think now with the perspective of a few more days I think that the few things that really stand out. One and I think

the most important thing is that after you know depending on how you count it 8 years n years of signaling that we had had a fundamental change in the relationship with China that China was a serious competitor. it was a potential threat, a

real threat to the United States and that we were going to significantly reorient the relationship, which is something that was a feature of the first Trump administration, but then really received bipartisan support um and continued during the Biden

administration and was very much a hallmark of the first, depending on how you want to count it, six to nine months of the second Trump administration. What we're seeing now is both leaders signaling that they want to take a step

back from the brink of the precipice and that they want to find ways to work together. And to me the the really big takeaway is that this was done by both leaders uh you know the Chinese by signaling an extraordinary level of

respect for President Trump um in terms of the arrangements they made the symbolism um of the the reception um and President Trump by showing this tremendous respect for uh Chairman Xi. each of them signaled that they want to find a way to have a effective

constructive relationship with each other. Now, that doesn't mean that we're going to be singing kumbaya. It doesn't mean that we're going to be loving each other and hugging trees um in anytime soon, but I think that it's quite

significant in terms of the overall messaging and the significance that it's coming from President Trump after he is seen as having fundamentally shifted the dynamic of the relationship um by taking us away from an effort at

being more cooperative to one of being more fiercely competitive. I think it's very very powerful. So to me that's what's really significant. The the specifics of what was discussed, what was agreed on, what China's going to do, what we're going to do are less

important than the fact that you have these two extremely powerful leaders who are ex very experienced, very confident, at the top of their games. um signaling I am the only one who can really effectively work with the other and it

is in the interest of both of our countries to find some motus for vendi that allows us to work together that uh so that's that is sort of this big strategic takeaway what is your sense about what actually was agreed to I mean there were there's

been we've seen slightly different issues coming out of both sides. The Boeing planes, the board of trade, uh $70 billion of US agricultural products. Even if the uh this is uh a secondary issue as you argue, it's there's still a

visible part of this and what also was. >> there's been a lot of debate about actually what was agreed to. what what is your ben best sense of what both sides agreed to actually do? >> So look, it's a very good question and

one of the things that's been a hallmark of recent exchanges with the Chinese is it's extremely hard to do a joint statement and you know for those of us who've had to negotiate joint statements at the leader level even when you're

doing it with very close allies or partners it can be quite hard. Um and you know I think the White House and uh the Chinese made a decision it wasn't worth it. Uh that always causes some complications because then you're left

with each side putting out its own statement and its own version of what happened. Ideally there's some coordination and my view is that the delay in putting the White House one out actually is a reflection of that. Um, part of it is there, and my

understanding is there were some comms issues with the plane as they were taking off, but I think part of it was they wanted to not be in a situation where they put something out and immediately had the Chinese say, "No, that's not true." So, we're left trying

to look at a number of different documents. First of all, I think the most important ones are the president's interviews with um Sean Hannity, which he did at the end of the first day and then he recorded an interview with Brett

Bear before he began the second day as I understand it and but it wasn't released. It was embargoed until he taken off. So those have the president's firthand assessment and description of what was discussed. Uh we also have the

White House fact sheet uh which I think is the one that in some ways reflects the most I suspect coordination with the Chinese uh when you read the languages in it. And then on the Chinese side you have a number of different things. So

you have first of all I think the most important one is Wangi who is simultaneously the uh member of the state council um the head of the party foreign affairs office and also the foreign minister um and he gave an interview which I suspect was somewhat

controlled um but where he answered a lot of questions and gave the Chinese readout in a way that sounds quite authentic. And then you also have the Ministry of Commerce, a mafcom in Beijing, which also appears to have done

a press statement that was picked up in the press as a MAFOM statement. So when you you put all those things together and you kind of triangulate between them, I think what's clear is that there was clearly discussion and I suspect

general agreement on um a purchases both soybeans, beef, I suspect some others, chicken um or poultry is I guess the term of art since I suspect turkeys may be involved too. Um, you have agreement on Boeings. Um, and sounds like the number is 200. I

would note that's less than people expected and like I'm sure you and others have seen, you know, Boeing stock fell when that number was announced because the markets expected a higher number, but the Chinese haven't challenged that. There's also

announcement on engines. Um, and that seems consistent with the numbers that were announced on aircraft. Uh, so I think what you have is the US being more specific, the Chinese being more elliptical on it and not suggesting that they committed to this,

which is a departure from how they've handled this stuff in the past um, over the years. But I think the part of that is because they don't want to make themselves vulnerable to the accusations that they're not following through. Um,

and but at the same time, I'm very confident they were discussed because I think they would have come out and said, "No, it's not true." Um, if they hadn't been given how specific the White House was. Uh, I think that the other

much President Chairman Xi's assessment that the way to manage the United States is through the relationship between the leaders and you know paradoxically or maybe not so paradoxically the US has more or less come to the same view. This

was, as I understand it, and I um President Obama's view at the end of his time in office. It was very much President Trump's view during his first term. It was very much President Biden's view. And that is that because of the

nature of the Chinese system, the only way to really effectively engage and have a high level of confidence that there will be followthrough is at the leader level. So the Chinese feel the same way. And I think that you know what

you see is you have two leaders who are very invested in the idea that they are the only one who can deal with the other and that that's a message that they want to send to their governments and to their peoples and that at the same time

they have a good relationship and can deal with each other. So to me that was the main message of the Chinese media. And I think that if you look carefully at what the White House said, the White House basically stuck to a very similar

line. I mean to me it's quite interesting. The president essentially read his toast, stayed very much on script. Um and in some of his public statements there was trying very very hard to stay on script. You saw much less spontaneity than you sometimes do.

And I think that that reflects his own sense that it was very important to convey respect and that he didn't want to he didn't want to do something which would run the risk of sort of distracting from the underlying message.

>> Yeah. Well, uh, one of the issues particularly that came from the Chinese side was, uh, President Xi's mention of this Thusidities trap and, uh, wonderful for many of us on the international relations side. um brings us back to the Pelpeneisian

war, the rise of Athens and the challenge of an incumbent power uh power in that case Sparta and quoting from Thusidities in his book the history of the Pelpeneisian war where he says quote it was the rise of Athens and the fear

that is instilled in Sparta that made war inevitable between Athens and Sparta. So, so let me just take a step back and ask you two related questions. One is what is the Thusidities trap? And then second, what was she potentially

getting at in uh in raising the issue? >> So, those are great questions and you know that I'm fascinated by this stuff, though I'm not an international relations person. I'm more of a my academic background limited as it is, is more history. Um but I think the

thusidity's trap is the idea that anytime there is the comparatively rapid emergence of a new power that that has the effect of upsetting existing power balances and you know this comes from an article and then a book by Graham

Allison and look I'm a huge Graham Allison fan but I'll just say it is rare that somebody has such an impact act in the world of ideas over such a long period of time. I mean basically if you go back to the essence of decision which

came out in 1971 and then in 2017 he's writing about the thusidities trap. It's pretty remarkable. But the idea is that anytime there's a significant shift amongst key players in a global order, not even a regional order or a bunch of

like bickering citystates that it runs the risk of the status quo power feeling threatened or the rising power feeling hemmed in by the status quo. What's really interesting and I I was you know I'm I'm fascinated by the fact that this

has been so embraced by the Chinese um and this is new though in the sense that I haven't heard this discussed in such detail um and emphasized so much by PRC media at leaderto meetings. Um but the Chinese glombmed on to this um both

because they like the underlying construct that the problem is the reaction of the established power um and also they like the idea that they're part of you know that a tradition um that in their mind recognizes the greatness and importance

of China. But as you know, Seth, and as we have discussed, what's interesting is the examples that Graham uses. And I mean, there's a whole sub genre of academic literature devoted to people attacking Graham um on this um you know,

because his examples are wrong, because he doesn't get one thing or another. But what I find most interesting is in most of the examples, the established power wins. So why did China >> including after >> including afterian war? >> Yeah. The

>> So it's like I'm not sure that it makes that much sense for our Chinese friends to highlight that because even if you assume this happens and the message is sort of America, it's on you not to make these mistakes. But the model and all

almost all of the examples, the status quo power wins and the rising power, the challenging power loses. Now, it may be that they're more comfortable talking about this because they see the US as blowing up the existing status quo,

which has benefited the US so much since World War II. Um, but I just find it interesting that they're embracing this. Now to me the good thing is is it's a signal that they understand and Xi Jinping himself understands how

important it is to figure out a way to avoid conflict. Now what I noticed is in the when the Chinese talk about this it's more about you United States need to find ways to avoid conflict rather than we China need to find ways to avoid

themselves with a rising power actually lost the war. Uh so probably not worth saying but quite ironic. What I do want to get to is Taiwan, which is there were there was a lot of discussion about whether Taiwan was going to get raised,

>> Look, I want to be very clear, Seth. I obviously wasn't in the meetings. I haven't talked in detail with anyone who was. And my sense is that in many ways the more important meeting was the one on day two um around the lunch, which

was much much smaller, which I would just note is very much how President Trump likes to do things. Um you know the first meeting what was striking was it was pretty big but they were all people who were very well known to the president. My experience is the

president is less comfortable with people he doesn't know in the room. Uh but that his preference is to do business in very very small um settings. I think it's very clear this came up. Look I I've been in a number of um US uh

PRC leader level meetings over the years. it always comes up, at least everyone I've been in. Uh the Chinese um the Chinese always feel compelled to raise it. Um and usually the structure is they go into a saliloquy about how

important Taiwan is, how it's got to be handled carefully, how if it's not handled carefully, there's a myriad of bad things that can happen, etc., etc., etc. Usually, the response is one of two things. one is we hear you and then

recitation the US one China policy based on the three joint communicates and the Taiwan relations act and in very recent years the six assurances is clear it is well known it has not changed you know blah blah blah um the US does not

support Taiwan independence like you know reciting our position also there have been times where the president has pushed back and said hey your behavior is causing instability. Your behavior, your aggressiveness is the root cause of the problem. Um there

was a time a long time ago where the Chinese would say you're violating the third communicate um which basically committed that US arm sales to Taiwan would go down over time but with caveat lang caveing language that essentially

we interpreted and we've said meant that this is only if China lowers its level of threat and it's based on Chinese behavior and that's allowed us to say the Chinese haven't done that and therefore we have to continue selling

weapons to Taiwan. But I think that the significant thing is my strong assumption is and in reading all the different readouts and hearing the president's interviews that seems to confirm that she raised this. I don't believe the president said well if you

do this for me I'll do this for you and for a couple of reasons. One is President Trump understands leverage. Um, I mean there are people who have who believe, oh, he doesn't understand the issues, understand how important it is

can't accept it or whatever the phrasing is. But they don't see Taiwan as something that they're going to bargain over because in their mind it's already done. Um Taiwan is theirs. It's just a question of when and how. Now I don't

understands China's position. If they thought there was an agreement, they would almost certainly say it. If they thought the US had committed to something, they would almost certainly say it. The fact that they're saying our

people on both sides of the street agree there is one China. Um, and that was true at that time. Uh my guess is that where we are now is different, but I don't believe that what Trump is saying is fundamentally different from the

reality. I mean, I think that every president has wanted to avoid a conflict. Every president has wanted to, you know, have their cake in it to have a dec have a good relationship with Taiwan and a good relationship with China. And every president knows there
